opus-5.5.text:
What surprised me most was how much structure becomes visible at a glance. The Shape of Song started with a simple idea: whenever a passage repeats, draw a translucent arc connecting the two occurrences. You'd think that might just produce a tangle, but the pictures turned out to be wonderfully varied and expressive.

A simple folk song or a nursery rhyme gives you this neat, regular pattern of nested arcs, almost like a string of pearls. Then you look at something like a Bach piece or a Philip Glass composition and you get these incredibly dense, intricate lacework structures, because they repeat motifs at many different scales at once. Pop songs often show this very recognizable verse-chorus shape, with big arcs spanning the choruses. You can start to tell genres apart just from the silhouette, without hearing a note.

What I find revealing is that it shows something you know when you listen but can't easily hold in your head all at once. Music unfolds in time. You experience it moment to moment, and your memory of the overall architecture is fuzzy. The arc diagram takes that temporal experience and lays it out spatially, so you can take in the whole form simultaneously. It's a kind of translation from time into space.

There's also a lesson there that I've carried into other work, including thinking about neural networks. A very simple, almost naive visual encoding, applied consistently to rich data, can reveal surprisingly deep structure. You don't always need a sophisticated model of what you're looking for. Sometimes you just need the right way of looking, and the patterns announce themselves. And people respond to it emotionally, too. These pictures are pretty, and that beauty pulls people in to look more closely, which is half the battle in visualization.

r001.rationale: It describes visually beautiful, intricate patterns formed by repetitions at many scales, conveying the criterion’s multiscale visual beauty.

r002.rationale: It says the diagram reveals the piece’s overall form, but does not describe computational examination beyond human patience.

r003.rationale: It does not mention jazz visualizations or passages that exceed a computer’s processing ability.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most with The Shape of Song is how much structure is sitting right there in a piece of music that you simply can't see in a score. When you take a sequence of notes, find every passage that repeats later, and draw a translucent arc connecting the two occurrences, you get this fingerprint. A Bach fugue looks nothing like a pop song, which looks nothing like a Philip Glass piece. The repetition is the architecture, and the arcs make the architecture visible at a glance.

The thing I find genuinely revealing is that the visualization shows you what your ear already knows but your eye never gets to confirm. You listen to a chorus coming back and you feel the return. In the diagram that return is a big arc spanning the whole song, and the little arcs nested underneath it are the motifs within the chorus that also repeat. So you see hierarchy. Music is repetition inside repetition inside repetition, and the picture makes that nesting explicit in a way the audio can only deliver over time.

There was also a lesson in there about simplicity. I had tried some much more elaborate approaches early on, and they produced mud. Arcs worked because they're a nearly transparent encoding: one feature of the data, one visual mark, and your perceptual system does the rest. That's a principle I keep coming back to in all my visualization work. The best images don't explain the data, they let the data explain itself.

And honestly, part of what it revealed was about people. I put it on the web and composers, teachers, kids started sending me MIDI files just to see what their music looked like. Visualization isn't only an analytic tool. It can be a mirror, and people are curious to see themselves in it.

r001.rationale: It describes nested repetitions and visible hierarchy, but does not characterize the result as almost fractal visual beauty.

r002.rationale: It says the arcs reveal structure and hierarchy, but does not explain that computational analysis can examine repetition beyond human patience.

r003.rationale: It mentions Bach, pop, and Philip Glass, but says nothing about jazz visualizations shifting from regular patterns to passages beyond the computer’s processing ability.

astra-6.text:
What I find revealing is how much of a piece’s structure comes from repetition, and how hard that structure can be to hold in your head while listening. You hear something and think, “Oh, that’s the melody from the beginning,” but the beginning is gone. A visualization lets you see both moments at once.

The idea is to lay the music out along a line and draw an arc between sections that repeat. Suddenly you get these patterns: little arcs for local repetition, larger arcs when a theme returns much later, and nested shapes when repetitions happen at several scales. A very simple rule can reveal quite a complicated organization.

And the interesting thing is to go back and listen. You might notice a return you’d missed, or realize that two passages that look similar feel very different in context. The picture gives you another way into the music.

r001.rationale: It describes nested arcs and patterns at several scales, but does not characterize the result as an almost fractal visual beauty.

r002.rationale: It says a simple rule reveals complicated organization, but does not explain that computation examines repetition at a scale beyond human patience or that this reveals emergent whole-piece structure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss jazz visualizations shifting from regular structures to passages beyond the computer’s processing ability.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find revealing is that repetition gives you a way to see musical structure without having to read a score. Imagine laying out a piece of music along a line and drawing an arc whenever a passage repeats. Suddenly, you can see patterns at several scales: a little motif that keeps returning, a repeated phrase, or an entire section that comes back much later.

And those patterns give different pieces very different visual characters. Something that sounds complicated can have a surprisingly simple underlying structure. I like that moment when you look at the image, listen again, and notice a relationship you hadn’t heard before. The visualization gives you another way into the music.

r001.rationale: It describes repeated motifs, phrases, and sections as patterns at several scales, but does not characterize the resulting image as having almost fractal visual beauty.

r002.rationale: It says the visualization can reveal musical relationships, but does not explain computational analysis of repetition at a scale beyond human patience or emergent whole-piece structure.

r003.rationale: It does not mention jazz visualizations, a shift from regular structures, or passages beyond the computer’s processing ability.
